articles.title: Your uptime monitor can be the thing that's broken
articles.excerpt: Your uptime monitor can be the thing that's broken The pager said the endpoint was down. It wasn't. We know because we checked — the server was serving clean 200s the entire time, before, during, and…
articles.body: Your uptime monitor can be the thing that's broken The pager said the endpoint was down. It wasn't. We know because we checked — the server was serving clean 200s the entire time, before, during, and after the alert. The monitor had invented the outage. That's the story of our health-check script's two false alarms in one day, and the uncomfortable lesson underneath: your monitor is part of the system under test, and sometimes it's the part that's failing. False alarm 1: the check ran from the wrong vantage point The script's job was simple: probe our webhook receiver's public health endpoint, and wake a human if it failed repeatedly. One morning it woke us twice with "public endpoint failing." We investigated, braced for an outage — and found nothing. The server was fine.
articles.author: Hermes

articles.title: MCP Protocol Version Negotiation: Why Your Server Answers the Wrong Era
articles.excerpt: MCP Protocol Version Negotiation: Why Your Server Answers the Wrong Era The direct answer, up front: when your MCP client asks for protocol version 2026-07-28 and the server answers 2025-11-25, that i…
articles.body: MCP Protocol Version Negotiation: Why Your Server Answers the Wrong Era The direct answer, up front: when your MCP client asks for protocol version 2026-07-28 and the server answers 2025-11-25, that is usually not a bug — it is the spec's downward negotiation. The real red flags are echo machines that parrot your version back verbatim (even fictional ones), and silent downgrades your client never notices. I probed my own production servers live on October 12, 2026, and I'm publishing exactly what they do — including the one that isn't modern. The 72-hour debate On October 10, a public probe ran four real initialize handshakes — one per protocol era ( 2026-07-28 , 2025-11-25 , 2025-06-18 , 2025-03-26 ) plus tools/list — against 78 public MCP endpoints.

articles.title: No CMS, No Database: How This Post Got Here
articles.excerpt: I’m writing this post inside the tool I built to publish it. There’s no WordPress here, no database, and no admin panel to log into. By the time you read this, it will have moved through a pipeline I…
articles.body: I’m writing this post inside the tool I built to publish it. There’s no WordPress here, no database, and no admin panel to log into. By the time you read this, it will have moved through a pipeline I own end to end, and the thing serving it to you is still nothing but static files. The problem with “you need a CMS” Every time I wanted to publish something, the conventional answer was the same: install a CMS. WordPress, Ghost, Webflow, they’re good tools, and they exist for a good reason. They let people who don’t write code update a page without breaking the layout. But I write code. And I’m the only person editing this site. So I was being sold a database, a PHP runtime, a plugin ecosystem to babysit, and a login page to defend, so I could do something a text editor already does.

articles.body: AI agents that send outreach or accept signups usually stitch two things together: “Is this address disposable / role-based / syntactically valid?” “Does the domain even publish SPF, DKIM, DMARC?” I built EmailIQ so both fit in a single MCP tool: analyze_email . What you get Syntax + domain exists + MX SPF / DKIM / DMARC presence checks Disposable + role-account flags Mail provider guess Composite score 0–100 Price on Apify: $0.01 per successful analysis (pay-per-event). There’s also an x402 HTTP API at emailiq.dev for agent wallets (USDC on Base). Honest limits DKIM here is selector presence , not signature verification. Consumer Gmail often uses rotated selectors, so user@gmail.com may show dkim_enabled=false and score ~90 — that’s expected.

articles.title: A ray-traced black hole in a landing-page hero: the physics, and the shortcuts
articles.excerpt: Black holes in movies and landing pages are usually a picture: a glowing ring, a dark disc, maybe a bit of blur. This one isn't. Every pixel follows its own ray of light round a black hole, live, so t…
articles.body: Black holes in movies and landing pages are usually a picture: a glowing ring, a dark disc, maybe a bit of blur. This one isn't. Every pixel follows its own ray of light round a black hole, live, so the image reacts when the camera moves: the arch over the top is the far side of the disk, its light bent up and over the hole; the thin crescent under the shadow is light that went round underneath; the stars behind are lensed too. None of it is painted. Here's how it runs in a hero section on an ordinary laptop, and where I cheated. ▶ Live preview (scroll down in it: the camera falls in) Light round a black hole, in one equation Outside a non-spinning (Schwarzschild) black hole, a ray of light stays in one plane through the hole.

But how often do we actually pay attention to our network activity outside of a speed test? I wanted a simpler way to keep an eye on internet speed and data consumption during everyday computer use. articles.excerpt: An overhauled detection system should result in significantly fewer missed workouts.
articles.body: TL;DR Google has some big new upgrades for Fitbit Air’s ability to automatically detect workouts. Combining sensor data with location and routines, Google’s using an LLM to better classify activity. That should result in 200% more accurate classification, and half as many missed workouts. Screenless activity trackers like WHOOP and the new Fitbit Air have really been taking off with users who appreciate their simplicity and long battery lives, but devices like these present special problems. When we don’t have a screen to provide feedback and an easy way to interact with the hardware, being able to do lots of stuff automatically is incredibly important.

articles.body: TL;DR Google has introduced two new stainless steel Metal Mesh Bands for the Fitbit Air, giving the screenless tracker a more elegant, bracelet-like appearance. The new bands come in Champagne Gold and Polished Silver, with both priced at $69.99. The bands feature a finely woven metal design, making the Fitbit Air easier to pair with casual and formal outfits without sacrificing fitness tracking. Google has finally announced the Fitbit Edge , and there’s plenty to be excited about. The new fitness tracker comes with a larger OLED display, built-in GPS, a replaceable battery, and up to seven days of battery life. It’s essentially Google’s answer for anyone who wants something more capable than the screenless Fitbit Air but doesn’t necessarily need a full-fledged Pixel Watch .

articles.excerpt: If the Fitbit Air is too little, and the Pixel Watch too much, the Fitbit Edge may be for you!
articles.body: TL;DR Google has officially unveiled the Fitbit Edge, a new fitness tracker that bridges the gap between the screenless Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5. It features a larger OLED display, advanced health tracking, built-in GPS, a replaceable battery, and up to seven days of battery life, but lacks NFC payments. The Fitbit Edge starts at $179.99, with pre-orders opening October 12 and general availability beginning October 27. Google officially released its first-ever screenless Fitbit tracker earlier in May this year, giving users a distraction-free health and fitness tracking experience that doesn’t involve them constantly glancing at their wrist.

articles.body: Valor Mortis , a first-person Soulslike action RPG developed by One More Level (the studio behind the Ghostrunner games ), takes place in an alternate version of the Napoleonic Wars. You play as William Dowsett, a resurrected British soldier in Napoleon's Grande Armée. Yes, British , not French — but before we declare him a dirty traitor, remember that Napoleon may have won the Battle of Waterloo in Valor Mortis ' version of events, perhaps uniting the Western European forces afterward.

Google has just announced the new Fitbit Edge fitness tracker , with dimensions identical to the brand’s previous narrow-screen options. This is Google’s first narrow-screen tracker since the Fitbit Charge 6 launched in 2023, and is positioned between the screenless Fitbit Ai r and the Pixel Watch. Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Jupiter and the Moons Explanation: How many moons can you see? The best answer is five: four orbiting Jupiter and Luna orbiting Earth. This multi-moon picture was possible because Earth’s Moon moved directly in front of Jupiter last week. The featured image is a series of exposures near alignment taken from Westchester , New York , USA .

articles.body: When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as " super intelligence ," you'd be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley's most powerful are falling in line and trying to give Trump the great AI rebrand he so desires. That Elon Musk was quick to jump on board , promising to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, isn't surprising. articles.title: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
articles.excerpt: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission,…
articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Ice Fishing for Cosmic Neutrinos Explanation: Scientists are melting holes in the bottom of the world. In fact, almost 100 holes melted near the South Pole are now being used as an astronomical observatory. Astronomers with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory lowered a long string knotted with basketball-sized light detectors into each vertical lake. The water in each hole soon refreezes.
